items.title: Picking a timeout for fetchPricing: too short vs. too long
items.description: L3's fix gives fetchPricing a 500ms timeout. Set it too low, and a pricing API that's merely slow (not actually broken) gets treated as failed, falling back to a stale price more often than necessary. Set it too high, and a genuinely hung dependency holds a connection open for longer before the fallback kicks in -- which is exactly the resource-exhaustion problem from L1's outage, just capped instead of unlimited. This chart shows the false-fallback rate assuming the pricing API's real response times are usually fast but occasionally spike, holding a worst-case hang at bay only once the timeout fires.
items.compute: const typicalP95Ms = 250; const spikeMs = 1200; const spikeShare = 0.08; let falseFallbackRate; if (params.timeoutMs >= spikeMs) { falseFallbackRate = 0; } else if (params.timeoutMs >= typicalP95Ms) { falseFallbackRate = spikeShare * (1 - (params.timeoutMs - typicalP95Ms) / (spikeMs - typicalP95Ms)); } else { falseFallbackRate = spikeShare + (1 - spikeShare) * (1 - params.timeoutMs / typicalP95Ms) * 0.5; } return { falseFallbackPercent: Math.max(0, Math.min(100, falseFallbackRate * 100)) };

outputs.label: Requests that fall back to a stale price unnecessarily

items.title: How many fault types are worth testing?
items.description: Per L3's prioritization trade-off, faults aren't equally likely or equally costly -- timeout/hang and error responses are common and high-impact (like L1's outage); malformed bodies and slow-but-not-hung responses are less common; truly exotic faults (a specific byte sequence, a specific ordering of two failures) are rare. This shows the returns from testing the most-likely faults first: coverage of realistic production incident types climbs fast for the first few fault types tested, then flattens -- the diminishing-but-real returns L3 argues for prioritizing by likelihood and impact instead of trying to cover everything.

params.name: faultTypesTested
params.label: Distinct fault types with a fault-injection test

items.compute: const maxCoverage = 92; const rate = 0.55; const coverage = maxCoverage * (1 - Math.pow(1 - rate, params.faultTypesTested)); return { incidentTypesCovered: coverage };

outputs.label: Real production incident types this would have caught
